title: Due Process for Derek Chauvin
author: Scott Yenor
content:
![Due Process for Derek
Chauvin](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/11/AP21111404557205.jpg)

> _American Scapegoat:  
> How a Corrupt Justice System Sacrificed Derek Chauvin to the Mob_  
> By T.J. Harker  
> Passage, 400 pages, $34.95

Derek Chauvin, the former Minneapolis police officer convicted of murdering
George Floyd in 2020, was stabbed twenty-two times while in federal custody.
Though he survived, he has become America's scapegoat--the title of T.J.
Harker's[ _meticulous new book_](https://passage.press/products/american-
scapegoat?ref=compactmag.com) on the Chauvin trial. Harker, a former assistant
US attorney, has prosecuted many such cases. Drawing on his experience, he
shows where the conventional narrative goes wrong.

As a strict legal matter, Chauvin's case is not about race relations, patterns
of police conduct, or any of the other controversies for which it was taken as
evidence. It is about whether Chauvin, in fact, committed a crime and received
a fair trial. In the American system, justice requires clear, rebuttable
charges brought before a neutral magistrate and an impartial jury that decides
on the basis of clear evidence, not hysteria or fear. The prosecution must
charge only what the evidence can bear, while giving the accused fair notice
of how the evidence will be organized. Exculpating evidence or material that
would impeach the state's own witnesses must also be given to the defense.

In the mob-like atmosphere that surrounds high-profile and politically charged
cases, these safeguards come under assault. Prosecutors playing to the crowd
can act unethically. Judges can bow to the mob too. No number of peremptory
challenges will change the fact that jury pools can hate the accused, refuse
to listen at trial, bow to the crowd, and preordain a conviction.
